e.etymology: Coined for the singer Kelis Rogers, whose parents blended their own names, Kenneth and Eveliss. The name spread in the US in the 2000s, when Milkshake (2003) was her biggest hit.

assoc.t: Kelis, the one-name singer of Milkshake

e.etymology: A spelling of Quincy, a Norman surname from places in France named for a Roman called Quintus, fifth. Quincey Morris is the Texan in Bram Stoker's Dracula; today it is given equally to girls and boys.

assoc.t: Quincey Morris, the Texan in Bram Stoker's Dracula

e.etymology: The feminine of Fabian, from the Roman family name Fabius, built on Latin faba, bean. It is used in Italy, Brazil and across Spanish-speaking countries.
A respelling of Ainsley, a surname from Annesley in Nottinghamshire or Ansley in Warwickshire, place names joining Old English words for solitary or hermitage with leah, woodland clearing.
A pet form of Vincent, from Latin vincens, conquering. In the US it has an Italian American ring, as a short form of Vincenzo too.
namesakes: Vinny Gambini (Joe Pesci's lawyer in My Cousin Vinny)

assoc.t: title character of My Cousin Vinny (1992)

e.note: Pop culture gives it a strong New York Italian American stereotype, from My Cousin Vinny to Jersey Shore.

e.etymology: From Arabic asim, protector or guardian, the active participle of the verb to protect. It is used from Bosnia and Turkey to Pakistan.

In India Ram is the everyday form of Rama, the seventh avatar of Vishnu and hero of the Ramayana; the Sanskrit word means pleasing. A separate Hebrew name Ram, high or exalted, belongs to an ancestor of King David.

assoc.t: Rama, hero-god of the Hindu epic Ramayana

e.note: The name is said RAHM, but Americans will read it as ram: the truck, the sheep, the verb.

e.etymology: From Sanskrit ishika, a reed, and by extension the arrow or the painter's brush made from one.
Usually a spelling of Reva, a Sanskrit name for the Narmada, one of India's sacred rivers. It can also be a form of Riva, a short form of Rivka, the Hebrew Rebecca.
The Italian form of Hilaria, from Latin hilaris, cheerful, the same source as Hilary and the word hilarious. It is a popular name in Italy.
A respelling of Luca, the Italian form of Luke, from Latin Lucas and Greek Loukas, man from Lucania in southern Italy. The final h matches Noah, Jonah and Micah.
A spelling of Nicole, the French feminine of Nicolas, from Greek Nikolaos: nike, victory, plus laos, people. The h follows Nicholas, and the spelling peaked in the US around 1980.
A spelling of Zachary, the English short form of Zachariah, from Hebrew Zekharyah, the Lord has remembered. In the Bible the name belongs to a prophet and to the father of John the Baptist.
A spelling of Kip, which began as a short form of Kipling, an English surname taken from a place name. Kipp is also a surname in its own right.

assoc.t: KIPP, a national network of public charter schools

e.etymology: A form of Persian Keyvan, the name of the planet Saturn. In the US it also arose independently, as Kay- joined to the -von of Javon and Davon.
namesakes: Kayvon Thibodeaux (New York Giants pass rusher)

e.etymology: A short form of Isabella, the Italian and Latinate form of Isabel, which began as a medieval Spanish form of Elizabeth, Hebrew for God is my oath. Sabella is also an Italian surname.
From Punjabi mehar, grace or blessing, especially the grace of God in Sikh prayer; the word comes from Persian mehr, kindness and affection. It is given mostly to girls.
A new surname-style name pairing the Win- of Winnie and Winslow with the -sley of Kinsley and Tinsley. Winsley is also a village in Wiltshire, England.

A respelling of Tristan, from the Celtic name Drystan, from drest, tumult, reshaped in Old French romance under the influence of triste, sad. Tristan is the knight who loves Iseult in Arthurian legend.
A variant of Mabel, from the medieval Amabel, Latin amabilis, lovable, respelled as if joining May and the French belle, beautiful. Mother Maybelle Carter made it a country music name.
namesakes: Maybelle Carter (guitarist and matriarch of country's Carter Family)

e.etymology: An African American coinage joining the De- prefix of DeAndre and DeAngelo to Shaun. Shaun is an English spelling of Irish Seán, the Irish John.
The Spanish and Portuguese feminine of Rafael, from Hebrew Refael, God has healed. Raphael is the archangel who heals Tobit in the Book of Tobit.
Coined in France at the end of the 1700s from Latin corallium, coral. It is popular in France and Quebec and has drawn American notice alongside Cora and Coraline.
A modern American name in the family of Makaiah and Makiyah, read by some as a form of the biblical Micaiah. It is given to boys and girls in near-equal numbers.

e.meaning: heaven spelled backward (in the spelling Nevaeh)
e.etymology: A respelling of Nevaeh, which is heaven written backward and took off after P.O.D. singer Sonny Sandoval gave it to his daughter in 2000.
e.note: With the a and e switched it no longer spells heaven backward, which is the point of Nevaeh.

e.etymology: A modern American blend of Ky-, as in Kyle and Kyla, with the -lynn ending.
A spelling of Raelynn, a 20th-century American combination of Rae and Lynn.
A respelling of Rylan, probably a form of the English surname Ryland, land where rye is grown. The Rh- borrows the look of Welsh names like Rhys.
From an English occupational surname for an archer, a man who fought or hunted with the bow.

assoc.t: Bowman baseball cards, a Topps brand

e.etymology: From the Turkic word temür, iron. It is the name of the 14th-century conqueror Timur, known in the West as Tamerlane, and is common from Turkey across Central Asia and Russia.
namesakes: Timur (14th-century Central Asian conqueror, also called Tamerlane)

e.etymology: Most likely a pared-down spelling of Emery or Emory, an English surname from medieval Germanic names such as Amalric and Heimrich. The Welsh name Emrys is unrelated.
From the English word trust, which came from Old Norse traust, confidence or protection. It is one of the newest virtue names, alongside Truth and True.
